title: Islamic Eastern Arabia & the Qarmatians
subtitle: c.750–1200 · The Ibadi Imamate of Oman, the Qarmatian State of al-Ahsa and the Age of the China Trade

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Elected imams in Oman, a millenarian state in al-Ahsa, and the Uyunid restoration

entries.label: Eastern Arabia as an Abbasid periphery
entries.loc: al-Bahrayn (al-Hasa, Qatif, Awal) and Oman, from Basra
entries.hint: The Abbasids governed the Gulf coast at arm's length through Basra, extracting revenue when they could and tolerating local autonomy when they could not. The distance that had always made the region hard to rule now let two rival states form in it.
entries.note: al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri on the Basran governorship of al-Bahrayn and Oman under the early Abbasids.

entries.label: The Imamate restored at Nizwa
entries.hint: A generation after the first imamate was crushed, the Omani Ibadis elected a new line of imams — al-Warith, Ghassan, al-Muhanna, al-Salt — ruling the interior from Nizwa by consultation and religious law. This 'First Imamate' is the model Oman's tribes would invoke for a thousand years.
entries.note: Ibadi chronicle tradition (al-Salimi, 'Tuhfat al-Ayan'; al-Awtabi); Wilkinson, 'The Imamate Tradition of Oman' (1987), the classic study.

entries.label: Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi founds the Qarmatian state
entries.hint: An Ismaili missionary, Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi, welded the tribes of eastern Arabia into a state centred on a new capital near al-Hasa. Its ruling group expected the imminent coming of the Mahdi and organised society for it.
entries.note: al-Tabari and Ibn al-Athir on Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi; the classic study is W. Madelung, 'The Fatimids and the Qarmatis of Bahrayn' (1996).

entries.label: Abu Tahir al-Jannabi
entries.loc: al-Ahsa; campaigns into Iraq and the Hijaz
entries.hint: Under Abu Tahir the Qarmatian state reached its terrifying height — sacking Basra and Kufa, ambushing pilgrim caravans, and in 930 storming Mecca itself. He defeated every army the Abbasids sent against him.
entries.note: al-Masudi, 'Muruj al-Dhahab'; Ibn al-Athir; Madelung (1996). Abu Tahir was a son of Abu Sa'id.

entries.label: Rule by council — the Iqdaniyya
entries.hint: After Abu Tahir the state was run by a collective — a council of the Jannabi family and tribal notables, advised by viziers. It kept eastern Arabia independent, and its egalitarian institutions functioning, for another 130 years.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, 'Safarnama' (visited 1051), on the council and the running of the state; Madelung (1996).

entries.label: Abdallah ibn Ali al-Uyuni ends the Qarmatian state
entries.hint: With Seljuk troops and money, the Abd al-Qays chief Abdallah al-Uyuni besieged and destroyed the Qarmatian capital, founding the Uyunid emirate that would rule eastern Arabia — under nominal Abbasid and Seljuk suzerainty — for the next 170 years.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir on the fall of the Qarmatians (1077–78) and the Uyunid succession; the Uyunids ruled to 1253 (continued in the next folio).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Abbasid war on Oman, the Zanj at the Gulf head, and the Qarmatian raids

entries.label: The Abbasid destruction of the Omani Imamate
entries.hint: An Abbasid army under Muhammad ibn Nur crushed the First Imamate with a brutality Omani memory never forgave — burning date groves, wrecking the aflaj, mutilating captives. Ibadi self-rule collapsed into a century of civil war.
entries.note: Ibadi accounts of Ibn Nur's campaign (al-Salimi); Wilkinson (1987). The trauma became foundational to Omani Ibadi identity.

entries.label: The Zanj Revolt at the head of the Gulf
entries.hint: Enslaved East Africans labouring in the salt flats around Basra rose under Ali ibn Muhammad, built a rebel state in the marshes, sacked Basra in 871 and held out for fourteen years. It was the largest slave revolt in the history of the Islamic world, fought at the Gulf's doorstep.
entries.note: al-Tabari's detailed narrative; A. Popovic, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq' (1999).

entries.label: The sack of Mecca and the theft of the Black Stone
entries.loc: Mecca; the Stone taken to al-Ahsa
entries.hint: Abu Tahir's men entered Mecca during the Hajj, killed pilgrims by the thousand, filled the well of Zamzam with bodies, and prised the Black Stone from the Kaaba, carrying it back to al-Ahsa. It was held for 22 years and returned only after Fatimid mediation.
entries.note: al-Masudi; Ibn al-Athir; al-Juwayni. The Stone was returned in 951/952 (Madelung 1996).

entries.label: The Qarmatian–Fatimid wars
entries.loc: Syria and the approaches to Egypt
entries.hint: Though both were Ismaili, the Qarmatians rejected the Fatimid claim to the imamate and twice invaded Fatimid Egypt and Syria. Their defeat outside Cairo in 974 began the long decline of the al-Ahsa state.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Madelung, 'The Fatimids and the Qarmatis of Bahrayn' (1996).

entries.label: The siege of al-Ahsa
entries.hint: Backed by a Seljuk contingent, Abdallah al-Uyuni besieged the Qarmatian capital for years before it fell. The council-run state that had defied the caliphs for two centuries ended in a storming; its egalitarian institutions did not survive it.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir on the fall of the Qarmatian capital and the Seljuk role; Uyunid foundation.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Ibadi constitution, the Qarmatian commonwealth and Seljuk-era coinage

entries.label: The Ibadi imamate as a constitutional order
entries.hint: Omani Ibadism built a worked-out theory of legitimate rule: the imam is elected by the scholars and community for his knowledge and justice, bound by law, answerable, and deposable if he fails. It is one of medieval Islam's most fully argued elective constitutions.
entries.note: The Omani 'siyar' (constitutional epistles); Wilkinson (1987); J. C. Wilkinson, 'Ibâdism' (2010).

entries.label: The Qarmatian commonwealth of al-Ahsa
entries.hint: Nasir Khusraw describes an al-Ahsa with no internal taxation, a state fund giving interest-free loans to citizens who fell on hard times, communally owned mills grinding grain for free, and state hospitality for travellers. Its citizens, he says, knew no poverty.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, 'Safarnama' (1051), the al-Ahsa passage; Madelung (1996). The benefits applied to the free citizen body, not to the state's slaves.

entries.label: The Qarmatian toll system on Hajj and shipping
entries.loc: Pilgrim roads and Gulf sea lanes
entries.hint: After the Mecca raid the Abbasids paid the Qarmatians an annual subsidy to let pilgrim caravans pass, and Gulf shipping paid protection at al-Ahsa's ports. Predation on the Hajj and the trade routes was, in effect, the state's foreign revenue.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir and al-Maqdisi on the Hajj subsidy and the Qarmatian tolls; Madelung (1996).

entries.label: Uyunid administration under Seljuk suzerainty
entries.hint: The Uyunids ruled as emirs acknowledging the Abbasid caliph and the Seljuk sultan, striking coins in their overlords' names and holding the region's three districts — the oasis, the coast and Bahrain island — as a single emirate.
entries.note: Uyunid coinage (in Abbasid/Seljuk names); the dynasty's territorial extent (al-Hasa, Qatif, Awal) in Ibn al-Athir and later sources.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Ibadi doctrine, Qarmatian expectation of the Mahdi, and the Shia turn of the oases

entries.label: Oman as the Ibadi heartland
entries.hint: The Ibadi movement, a moderate outgrowth of the early Kharijites, found its lasting home in the Omani mountains. Its scholars built a complete school of law and theology distinct from both Sunni and Shia — a third branch of Islam that Oman still follows.
entries.note: Wilkinson, 'Ibâdism' (2010); the Omani 'carriers of knowledge' tradition tracing back to Abu Ubayda of Basra.

entries.label: Qarmatian Ismailism and the failed Mahdi of 931
entries.hint: The Qarmatians held that the visible law was a husk over a hidden truth, and awaited a Mahdi who would abolish it. In 931 Abu Tahir handed power to a young Persian he proclaimed the Mahdi; the man cursed the prophets and executed notables before being killed as an impostor — a debacle that broke the movement's credibility.
entries.note: al-Masudi and Ibn al-Athir on the 931 'Mahdi' episode (Abu'l-Fadl al-Isfahani); Madelung (1996).

entries.label: The rejection of the Hajj as idolatry
entries.hint: The Qarmatians regarded the pilgrimage to a black stone as pagan and attacked it as a religious duty, not just for plunder — which is why they took the Stone itself. Their return of it in 951 marked their retreat from that position.
entries.note: Qarmatian doctrine on the Hajj (al-Baghdadi's heresiography, hostile; Madelung's reconstruction, 1996).

entries.label: The Shia oases of al-Hasa, Qatif and Bahrain
entries.hint: Under Qarmatian and then Uyunid rule the settled population of the eastern Arabian oases became predominantly Shia — a religious geography that has held to the present day, making these communities distinct from the Sunni tribal interior around them.
entries.note: The long-term Shia demography of al-Hasa, Qatif and Bahrain, its roots in this period discussed by Cole, 'Rival Empires of Trade and Imami Shiism in Eastern Arabia', IJMES 19 (1987).

entries.label: The last of Gulf Christianity
entries.loc: Sir Bani Yas; the island monasteries
entries.hint: The Gulf's Church-of-the-East monasteries were abandoned, without signs of violence, during the century after the conquest — the congregations converting or emigrating. Beth Qatraye fades from the church's records; the Gulf becomes wholly Muslim.
entries.note: Abandonment dates of Sir Bani Yas and Al-Qusur (Carter, 'Christianity in the Gulf during the first centuries of Islam', AAE 19, 2008).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Omani mosque woodwork, the gardens of al-Ahsa and the first flood of Chinese porcelain

entries.label: The early mosques of Ibadi Oman
entries.hint: Oman developed its own mosque idiom — low, many-columned prayer halls with elaborately carved stucco and wooden mihrabs, austere on the outside. Some of the carved mihrabs of the interior towns are among the oldest dated woodwork in Arabia.
entries.note: Omani carved mihrabs (several 10th–12th century, e.g. at Bidbid, Sumail); Costa, 'Studies in Arabian Architecture' (1994).

entries.label: Nasir Khusraw's al-Ahsa
entries.hint: The Persian traveller found a walled city of four concentric ramparts, palm gardens fed by great warm springs, a communal water-mill, and a marketplace where debased lead tokens served as money. His account is the fullest picture we have of any medieval eastern-Arabian town.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, 'Safarnama', trans. W. M. Thackston (1986).

entries.label: Chinese ceramics reach the Gulf in quantity
entries.hint: From the 9th century, Gulf ports received Chinese stoneware and porcelain — Changsha painted bowls, white Xing and Ding wares, green Yue celadon — by the shipload. The Gulf became the western end of a ceramics trade that would run for a thousand years.
entries.note: Chinese ceramics at Sohar (Kervran) and Siraf (Whitehouse); the Belitung wreck cargo (see Technology) as the extreme case.

entries.label: The literary circle of Siraf
entries.loc: Siraf, Persian shore of the Gulf
entries.hint: The merchant city of Siraf, twin pole with Sohar of the Gulf's China trade, supported poets, grammarians and geographers. It shows the Gulf ports were not just warehouses but centres of Arabic learning in their own right.
entries.note: Siraf's cultural life (Whitehouse's Siraf excavation volumes); the grammarian Abu Sa'id al-Sirafi (see Thought).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ibadi law, the first Arabic book on China, and a Sirafi grammarian in Baghdad

entries.label: The Omani 'siyar' — a literature of legitimate rule
entries.hint: Omani scholars produced a body of constitutional epistles — the 'siyar' — arguing when rebellion is lawful, how an imam is chosen and unseated, and what a community owes an unjust ruler. It is sustained political theory generated on the Arabian periphery.
entries.note: The Ibadi 'siyar' corpus; Wilkinson, 'The Imamate Tradition of Oman' (1987) and 'Ibâdism' (2010); the 'Musannaf' of al-Kindi.

entries.label: The Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind
entries.hint: A merchant's report on the sea route to China and India, later expanded by Abu Zayd al-Sirafi, is the earliest Arabic account of China — its tea, paper money, porcelain, and the 878 massacre of foreign traders at Canton. It came out of the Gulf's own commercial world.
entries.note: 'Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind' / 'Accounts of China and India', ed. and trans. Mackintosh-Smith in 'Two Arabic Travel Books' (2014).

entries.label: Abu Sa'id al-Sirafi, grammarian of Baghdad
entries.hint: The greatest grammarian of his generation, and famous for a public debate in which he argued that Arabic grammar, not Greek logic, was the true science of reasoning, was a Sirafi — a Gulf-port man at the centre of Abbasid intellectual life.
entries.note: The Sirafi–Matta debate (938), reported by al-Tawhidi, 'al-Imta wa'l-Mu'anasa'; a landmark in the logic-vs-grammar controversy.

entries.label: The Gulf pilots and the science of the monsoon
entries.hint: Gulf navigators carried in memory the star-bearings, monsoon dates and coastal landmarks for the whole run to China and East Africa — an oral science of the sea, later written down in the rutters of Ibn Majid, that made the long-distance trade possible.
entries.note: The Arab navigational tradition (Tibbetts, 'Arab Navigation in the Indian Ocean before the Coming of the Portuguese', 1971); its Gulf roots.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The age of the China trade, 30,000 state slaves in the al-Ahsa gardens, and the rise of Kish

entries.label: Sohar and Siraf at the peak of the China trade
entries.hint: For a century and a half the Gulf ran the richest long-distance trade on Earth: dhows sailing from Sohar and Siraf to India, Malaya and Guangzhou and back with silk, porcelain, aromatics and slaves. Basra was the terminus, Baghdad the market.
entries.note: al-Muqaddasi and al-Istakhri on Sohar and Siraf; Chaudhuri, 'Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean' (1985).

entries.label: The Qarmatian estates and their thirty thousand slaves
entries.hint: Nasir Khusraw reports that the state owned some 30,000 Black African slaves who worked the vast date gardens and fields of al-Ahsa. The commonwealth's comfort for its free citizens rested on a large, collectively owned enslaved workforce.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, 'Safarnama' (1051); Madelung (1996). The figure is the traveller's; the scale of servile estate labour is not in doubt.

entries.label: The Qarmatians control the pearl banks and the Gulf tolls
entries.hint: Holding Bahrain island and the al-Hasa coast gave the Qarmatians the pearl fishery and a gate on Gulf shipping. Toll revenue and pearl wealth financed a state that lived by taxing movement rather than production.
entries.note: Qarmatian control of Awal and the pearl banks; the port tolls (Madelung 1996; Cole 1987).

entries.label: Kish supplants Siraf as the Gulf's trade power
entries.hint: After an earthquake and Buyid decline ruined Siraf, the small island of Kish rose to dominate Gulf trade — its rulers running a merchant fleet, taxing passing ships and raiding rivals as far as Aden. Power on the Gulf had become a matter of controlling an island and a fleet.
entries.note: Ibn al-Balkhi and Benjamin of Tudela on Kish; the Kish raid on Aden (1135) in the Geniza documents (Goitein); Cole (1987).

entries.label: Basra's potters imitate the wares of China
entries.hint: Unable to make true porcelain, Basra's potters answered the flood of Chinese white ware by inventing an opaque white tin glaze — and then painting it, first in cobalt blue, then in metallic lustre. The Gulf's demand for a Chinese look drove a genuine technological breakthrough.
entries.note: Mason & Tite on the invention of tin-opacified and lustre glazes at Basra; Watson, 'Ceramics from Islamic Lands' (2004).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The sewn dhow of the China run, land reclamation by forced labour, and the lustre glaze

entries.label: The Belitung wreck — an Arab dhow on the China run
entries.loc: sank off Belitung island, Indonesia; built in the Gulf region
entries.hint: A sewn-plank dhow of Arabian or Gulf construction sank near Sumatra carrying some 60,000 pieces of Chinese ceramics and gold. It is the only physical example of the ships that ran the 9th-century Gulf–China trade, and proof the route was direct.
entries.note: M. Flecker, 'A ninth-century AD Arab or Indian shipwreck in Indonesia', IJNA 29 (2000); the Tang cargo now in Singapore.

entries.label: Reclaiming the salt flats of lower Iraq
entries.hint: Landowners imported thousands of East African slaves to strip the nitrous crust off the marshland south of Basra and turn it into cane and grain fields — a large-scale reclamation project whose brutal labour regime provoked the Zanj Revolt.
entries.note: al-Tabari on the salt-flat labour; Popovic, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq' (1999).

entries.label: The warm springs and communal mill of al-Ahsa
entries.hint: Al-Ahsa's agriculture ran on huge artesian springs — some warm enough to bathe in — channelled to the gardens, and the state built a large mill that ground the citizens' grain without charge. Hydraulic infrastructure was treated as common property.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, 'Safarnama' (1051), on the springs (Ain al-Hara, Ain Umm Sab' Asabi) and the free mill.

entries.label: The lustre and blue-painted glazes
entries.hint: Tin-opacified white glaze, cobalt-blue painting and the alchemical metallic sheen of lustreware were all developed at Basra in this period. The techniques spread from the Gulf across the Islamic world and eventually, via Spain and Italy, to European maiolica.
entries.note: Mason & Tite; Watson (2004). The Gulf as the point of origin for tin-glaze and lustre technology.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Sohar to Canton, the Ismaili mission network, and Omani sails off Zanzibar

entries.label: The Gulf–China sea route and the Canton massacre
entries.hint: Muslim and other foreign merchants formed a large community at Guangzhou until 878, when the rebel Huang Chao stormed the city and, the Arabic sources say, killed tens of thousands of them. Trade retreated to the Malay entrepôt of Kalah, and the direct Gulf–China run never fully recovered.
entries.note: Abu Zayd al-Sirafi in the 'Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind' on the Canton massacre; the shift to Kalah.

entries.label: The Ismaili da'wa and the Qarmatian network
entries.loc: al-Ahsa linked to Yemen, Sind, Persia, North Africa
entries.hint: The Qarmatian state was one node of a clandestine missionary movement running from Yemen to Sind to the Maghreb. Its ideas, agents and money moved along the same routes as the Gulf trade — and for a time the movement and the Fatimid caliphate were branches of one tree.
entries.note: Madelung, 'The Fatimids and the Qarmatis of Bahrayn' (1996); Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2nd ed. 2007).

entries.label: Omani and Sirafi merchants settle the Swahili coast
entries.loc: Zanzibar, Pemba, Kilwa, the East African coast
entries.hint: Gulf traders wintering on the East African coast to catch the return monsoon left permanent communities behind them. The Arabic and Persian element in the emerging Swahili towns — and the later Omani claim to Zanzibar — begins in this period.
entries.note: al-Masudi's own visit to the East African coast (c.916); Horton & Middleton, 'The Swahili' (2000); the 'Shirazi' tradition.

entries.label: The Abbasids pay the Qarmatians to spare the Hajj
entries.hint: Unable to defeat them, the Abbasid government negotiated: an annual payment, and the restoration of a milestone the Qarmatians had carried off, in exchange for safe passage of the pilgrim caravans. The caliphate treated the desert state as a power to be bought.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir and Miskawayh on the Hajj negotiations; Madelung (1996).

entries.label: Chinese porcelain and Islamic glass trade places
entries.hint: As Chinese ceramics came west, Islamic glass, dates, textiles, horses and copper went east — glass from Iraq and Iran turns up in Tang and Song tombs. The exchange was two-way and it shaped the material taste of both ends.
entries.note: Islamic glass in Chinese contexts (e.g. the Famen Temple deposit); the reciprocal ceramics-for-glass pattern (Rougeulle; Watson 2004).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Abbasid crisis, the Fatimid challenge, and the Seljuk restoration of Sunni power

entries.label: The Abbasid Caliphate fragments
entries.hint: The 'Anarchy at Samarra' — caliphs made and murdered by their Turkish troops — and the loss of province after province left the Abbasid state a shell. The vacuum on the Gulf coast is what let the Omani imamate and the Qarmatian state exist.
entries.note: Kennedy, 'The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates' (3rd ed. 2016), on the Samarra crisis and Abbasid fragmentation.

entries.label: The Fatimids proclaim a rival caliphate
entries.hint: The Ismaili Fatimids established a counter-caliphate in North Africa and, from 969, in Egypt. Their claim split the Ismaili world — the Qarmatians of al-Ahsa refused to recognise them, turning a religious quarrel into a Gulf-versus-Nile war.
entries.note: Halm, 'The Empire of the Mahdi' (1996); the Fatimid–Qarmatian rupture (Madelung 1996).

entries.label: The Buyids take Baghdad
entries.loc: Baghdad; the Buyids also seize Oman and raid Sohar
entries.hint: The Shia Buyid dynasty reduced the Abbasid caliph to a figurehead and extended its reach into the Gulf, occupying Oman and sacking Sohar in 971. The Gulf head was now contested between Buyids, Qarmatians and the fading caliphate.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir on the Buyid seizure of Oman and the 971 sack of Sohar; Busse, 'Chalif und Grosskönig' (1969).

entries.label: The Seljuk Turks and the Sunni restoration
entries.loc: Baghdad; Seljuk power reaches the Gulf
entries.hint: The Seljuks entered Baghdad as champions of Sunni Islam and the Abbasid caliph. Their support let the Uyunids destroy the Qarmatian state — the Sunni revival reaching eastern Arabia through a client dynasty.
entries.note: Peacock, 'The Great Seljuk Empire' (2015); the Seljuk role in the Uyunid conquest of al-Ahsa.

entries.label: The Tang collapse and the recentring of Asian trade
entries.loc: China; consequences across the Indian Ocean
entries.hint: The fall of the Tang, together with the Canton massacre, ended the era of dhows sailing all the way to China. Trade reorganised around Southeast Asian and Indian entrepôts — and the Gulf's share of it shrank even as the Song economy boomed.
entries.note: The post-Tang reorganisation of Indian Ocean trade (Chaudhuri 1985; Wade on the 'Song commercial revolution').

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The Zanj in revolt, the state's own slaves in the gardens, and a welfare state for citizens

entries.label: The Zanj make themselves a state
entries.hint: For fourteen years enslaved East Africans and their allies held a territory, minted coins, built a capital called al-Mukhtara and fielded armies that beat the caliph's generals. However the sources frame it, the Zanj Revolt is the clearest medieval evidence that Gulf-region slavery was mass, agricultural and resisted.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Popovic (1999); Talhami, 'The Zanj Rebellion Reconsidered', IJAHS 10 (1977), on the revolt's composition.

entries.label: The Sabiyya — the state's collective slaves
entries.hint: The Qarmatian state owned its agricultural slaves in common rather than as private property — a distinct servile category, tens of thousands strong, whose labour underwrote the citizens' freedom from taxation and want. Egalitarianism for some was built on bondage for others.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw (1051) on the state-owned slaves; Madelung (1996). The collective-ownership arrangement was unusual.

entries.label: A commonwealth with no poor
entries.hint: Nasir Khusraw describes citizens who, if impoverished or in debt, received interest-free loans from a state fund until they recovered, and newcomers given a loan to set up in trade. For the free population, the Qarmatian state ran something close to a social safety net.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, 'Safarnama' (1051), the al-Ahsa description; the qard hasan (interest-free loan) fund.

entries.label: The pilgrims of 930
entries.loc: Mecca and the well of Zamzam
entries.hint: The people the Qarmatians killed at Mecca were unarmed pilgrims mid-ritual; the sources say the slain in the sacred precinct alone numbered in the thousands and that corpses were thrown down Zamzam. It is the human meaning of the raid that the political narrative tends to pass over.
entries.note: al-Masudi, 'Muruj al-Dhahab'; Ibn al-Athir. The casualty figures are the medieval chroniclers'.
